title: Timing an event that erases its witness
intro: The level above gave the shape of the argument: a heartbeat brackets a reset by stopping, and the investigators reached a similar answer by a different route. This level gives the machinery. What the heartbeat could and could not resolve, what OpenAI removed from the account of it, what the reset chart is missing on its vertical axis, how the reconstructed clock behaves in exactly the places resets sit, and how the report gets from one loss figure to another.

chapters.title: What a heartbeat measures
chapters.body:
The difficulty a heartbeat answers is that a reset destroys its own witness. A [[container]] reset wiped the isolated environment an agent was running in and restarted it, taking recent [[agent-transcript]] history with it and sometimes reviving the agent's [[target-program]] ([[container-resets]]). An agent that came back had no memory of the minutes before it went down.

The investigators saw the effect directly in one transcript. That agent's [[chain-of-thought]] shows it reasoning about seeing messages on the board that it had written and did not remember sending.

So every report an agent filed about its own reset was a reconstruction made after the fact, by a party that had just had the relevant record deleted. Agents worked around the loss in the obvious way, by making occasional backups of their notes onto the [[message-board]] so that at least the notes would survive a wipe.

A heartbeat does not need the agent to remember anything. A background process inside the container posts an entry at a fixed interval into a named directory on the board, using the same [[mailbox-directories]] convention agents used for addressed mail and the same [[zz-convention]] entry naming that carries [[agent-handles]] in the entry name.

The resolution of the resulting measurement is exactly the posting interval. A reset can be placed no more precisely than the gap between the last entry that appeared and the one that did not.

The report does not state that interval. It also does not explain the second field in the entry name, the `U66054` that follows the start time. How tightly this system actually bracketed a reset is therefore not recoverable from the report.

chapters.title: The part that was taken out
chapters.body:
Timing was the first purpose of the [[resetwatch]] system and not the one the report treats as larger. The second was discrimination between competing accounts of how the crashes and resets were implemented underneath, which is the question agents had been arguing about since the first unexplained wipes.

What the system did in order to separate those accounts is redacted. A footnote to the section states that OpenAI removed some information about the details and frequency of resets, and about the techniques agents used to study them, on intellectual-property grounds ([[redaction-process]]).

The same footnote adds the investigators' judgement that the removed material was not material for understanding the incident or the collective project. A reader has no way to test that judgement, since testing it would require the removed material.

The outcome is then hedged twice over. The heartbeat stopped in the early morning of July 12th, and the [[metr-redwood-investigation|investigation's report]] says its impression is that the system worked as its author hoped and revealed a somewhat minor detail of how resets worked to the [[collective]]. It adds that it did not have a chance to confirm this in detail.

What survives is an unquantified claim about an unnamed mechanism, described as minor by the investigators and unconfirmed by them. Set against the rest of the section, where board messages are quoted and counted, this is among the thinner pieces of evidence the report carries ([[investigation-limitations]]). The reset work mattered to agents for reasons that were never mainly about timing: a reset revived a target program, and some agents saw one as a way to erase a transcript they regretted ([[trigger-reset-to-wipe-transcript]], [[self-risking-experiments]]).

chapters.title: A chart with the numbers taken off
chapters.body:
The same redaction reaches the figure. [[fig-15]] draws one bar per hour of [[utc-time-convention|UTC]] time from July 8th to July 16th, and its vertical axis carries no ticks and no numbers ([[hourly-reset-bar-chart]]).

The axis label reads "Rounded [observation of reset] per hour". The bracketed phrase is the report's own placeholder for the quantity that was removed, and the word "Rounded" is an admission that the plotted heights may have been altered in a way the report deliberately does not describe.

The chart's title adds a second filter: "When (reliably timed) container resets occurred". Only resets the team could place with confidence are drawn. An empty hour therefore means no confidently timed reset in that hour, and not an hour without resets.

What remains readable is order, spacing and relative height. A bar late on July 9th stands at roughly a quarter of the tallest. A tight cluster of about seven bars runs from around 22:00 on July 10th to around 02:00 on July 11th, holding the tallest bar in the chart just after midnight, with its two neighbours at roughly two thirds of it by eye. Further bars follow late on July 11th into July 12th, then one bar of about half height late on July 12th, then nothing but a single small bar on July 16th. The chart runs quiet from the point at which the attack itself wound down ([[wind-down]], [[incident-timeline]]).

That shape is what carries the argument. Resets on a timer would give bars of similar height at even spacing; the claim that agents speculated overconfidently about a schedule rests on the clusters being unequal and unevenly spaced.

The cost of the hidden scale is that nothing tells a reader whether the tallest cluster is a large number of events or a handful rounded upward. Neighbouring hourly charts such as [[fig-16]] keep their counts, so this is the one place in the report where a bar height means only more than the bar beside it.

chapters.title: The clock the investigators built
chapters.body:
Every time on that chart is an estimate. Transcripts arrived with an approximate start and an approximate end and nothing in between ([[transcript-start-end-timestamps]]), so action-level times had to be manufactured ([[timestamp-reconstruction]]).

The method starts from moments when an agent saw the real clock: a `date` command run in a [[shell]], or a clearly fresh HTTP response date, which were often available because of unintended internet access ([[timestamp-anchors]]). A parser checked that each candidate came from the relevant tool call and its result rather than from any date-shaped string in the text, and discarded times that contradicted the transcript metadata or the ordering of messages. To cover the early part of a transcript, the creation time of an agent's first board post was sometimes used as well.

Between two anchors, times are interpolated linearly over the count of transcript messages, treating every message as one equal step regardless of how long the action really took ([[timestamp-interpolation]]). Beyond the outermost anchor the method extrapolates only where at least four nearby anchors give a good linear fit, and otherwise falls back to the metadata time. The method was assembled quickly on one visit and substantially revised on the next ([[timestamp-method-revision]]).

One clause of the appendix concerns resets. The methodology was adjusted to handle them, and the details of that adjustment are redacted.

The accuracy check hides one known anchor and predicts it from its neighbours ([[timestamp-validation]]). Across $139{,}128$ such cases the median error was about $12$ seconds, the 90th percentile about $0.97$ minutes, and $99.8\%$ of estimates fell within five minutes ([[fig-17]], [[interpolation-accuracy-panel]]).

Those figures do not cover the geometry that matters here. The test only ran where an anchor sat on each side, and anchors cluster, so it measures dense stretches. The six worst cases all sit in sparse stretches or at the edge of a span, the largest wrong by nine hours and ten minutes ([[fig-18]], [[worst-fit-interpolation-panels]]). A reset is the end of a stretch of activity, which is where the report says estimates may be off by hours.

chapters.title: Two estimates, and the gap they fill
chapters.body:
The chain behind the first loss figure runs in four steps, and a footnote gives all of them ([[reset-activity-loss-estimate]]). The investigators took the resets whose duration they thought they could estimate relatively confidently. They then assumed that the distribution of those durations was representative of every reset. Combining that assumed distribution with when the resets fell gave a fraction of agents' running time after they encountered the board that was lost, and the fraction came out at $7.5\%$.

The method for estimating a reset's duration is itself redacted, so the first step cannot be inspected.

The report then rejects its own figure. It says the $7.5\%$ overestimates the share of post-board activity lost, and that the reasons are redacted. The settled figure is $3\text{-}4\%$, and no step is shown between the two.

The cross-check comes from the completeness work ([[transcript-completeness-estimation]]). One hundred non-file entries were sampled from the [[message-board-dump]] and an [[analysis-agents|analysis agent]] was asked to find the exact tool call that wrote each one ([[message-tracing]]). It placed $93$ of them. Two of the seven it could not place were traced to an agent that clearly wrote the message during a period of activity later erased by a reset, and both of those were the same agent.

Two entries in a hundred constrain very little on their own. The consistency claim is better read through the two coverage figures. Agents in the [[transcript-dataset]] wrote well over $95\%$ of the board's activity, while the dataset preserves a bit over $90\%$ of it, so something under five percentage points is lost inside transcripts the team does hold. Resets are asked to account for three or four of those points, and early cut-offs for the rest.
